title: EBS is persistent block storage within one AZ
layout: Module 09 panels with functional conceptual diagrams

sections.heading: Attach inside the AZ
sections.text: An EBS volume is a network block device. Attach it to a compatible EC2 instance in the same Availability Zone; most volumes have one attached instance. Multi-Attach is a specific io1/io2 exception.

sections.heading: Reattach or restore
sections.text: Detach safely and reattach within the same AZ. To move to another AZ, create a snapshot and restore a new volume in the target AZ; a volume itself does not span AZs.

sections.heading: Plan persistence and performance
sections.text: A volume can outlive its instance, depending on Delete on termination. Resize with supported Elastic Volumes operations, extend the OS filesystem, and check the instance EBS bandwidth.

remember: Persistence, AZ scope and attachment rules are separate design decisions.

title: EBS: choose the disk for the access pattern
layout: Module 09 panels with functional conceptual diagrams

sections.heading: General-purpose SSD
sections.text: gp2 and gp3 balance price and performance for transactional applications, boot disks and general workloads.

sections.heading: Provisioned-IOPS SSD
sections.text: io1/io2 suit sustained IOPS demand. io2 Block Express targets stronger durability and consistent low latency.

sections.heading: Throughput-oriented HDD
sections.text: st1 serves frequent sequential processing; sc1 serves colder throughput workloads. Both exclude boot-volume use.

remember: Choose the access pattern before the volume type.

title: gp2 and gp3 separate capacity from performance differently
layout: Module 09 panels with functional conceptual diagrams

sections.heading: Capacity-linked gp2
sections.text: Smaller gp2 volumes use a credit balance for bursts. Capacity, IOPS and throughput must be evaluated together.

sections.heading: Independent gp3 controls
sections.text: gp3 includes a baseline and permits additional IOPS and throughput within configuration constraints; capacity alone need not buy performance.

sections.heading: Consistent io2 performance
sections.text: Check I/O size, required latency and the complete instance-to-volume path; a published maximum is not an application guarantee.

remember: Capacity, IOPS, throughput and latency are different constraints.

title: Find the narrowest point in the EBS path
layout: Module 09 panels with functional conceptual diagrams

sections.heading: Application demand
sections.text: I/O size and queue depth change the relation between operations per second and transferred bytes.

sections.heading: Volume limits
sections.text: Inspect latency, queueing and throughput alongside provisioned IOPS. A large sequential read behaves differently from small random writes.

sections.heading: Instance limits
sections.text: Use suitable EBS-optimized instances and verify the instance bandwidth/IOPS ceiling before increasing the volume specification.

remember: Measure every link before paying to widen one.

title: Snapshots capture changed blocks, not application intent
layout: Module 09 panels with functional conceptual diagrams

sections.heading: Incremental blocks
sections.text: The first snapshot includes written blocks; later snapshots capture changes. Deleting an earlier snapshot does not automatically invalidate later snapshots.

sections.heading: Application consistency
sections.text: Flush and quiesce appropriately before capture. Detachment is not mandatory; coordinate the database and all related volumes.

sections.heading: Managed snapshot storage
sections.text: Snapshots are EBS-managed recovery resources backed by S3; they are not ordinary objects in a customer-accessible snapshot bucket.

remember: A block snapshot is only as application-consistent as its capture procedure.

title: Restore in the target AZ and plan first-read latency
layout: Module 09 panels with functional conceptual diagrams

sections.heading: Restore into a new volume
sections.text: The restored volume must be created in the required AZ and attached to a compatible instance.

sections.heading: Initialize the working data
sections.text: First-read initialization can affect latency after restoring a snapshot. Test startup and application recovery rather than only volume creation.

sections.heading: Accelerate deliberately
sections.text: FSR, manual block reads and provisioned-rate initialization solve different timing/cost needs; their constraints are compared separately.

remember: Volume creation is not proof of application recovery readiness.

title: Automate recovery points with the right policy service
layout: Module 09 panels with functional conceptual diagrams

sections.heading: Target with tags
sections.text: DLM policies can target supported instances or volumes and create EBS snapshots or EBS-backed AMIs.

sections.heading: Schedule and retain
sections.text: Creation, retention, deletion and supported copy rules must match recovery and compliance requirements.

sections.heading: Choose the governance scope
sections.text: AWS Backup offers wider supported-service governance; successful backup creation must be followed by restore testing.

remember: Retention policies are useful only when the recovery points can be restored.

title: Encryption needs a working recovery key
layout: Module 09 panels with functional conceptual diagrams

sections.heading: Regional default setting
sections.text: Encryption by default applies prospectively to new volumes and snapshot copies in that account/Region.

sections.heading: Existing data needs migration
sections.text: Use an encrypted snapshot copy or encrypted new volume from a snapshot, then test and cut over. Enabling the setting does not alter old volumes.

sections.heading: Authorize the recovery key
sections.text: KMS policies and IAM permissions must permit the intended source, destination and recovery principals; cross-account keys need particular care.

remember: Test key access as part of recovery, not after a failure.

title: Multi-Attach shares a block device, not a normal file share
layout: Module 09 panels with functional conceptual diagrams

sections.heading: Shared block device
sections.text: Each attached instance can read and write the same blocks. Multi-Attach is not an NFS/SMB server.

sections.heading: Supported attachment scope
sections.text: Up to 16 supported Nitro instances in one AZ; Linux supports io1/io2, Windows supports io2. Check current instance and driver requirements.

sections.heading: Coordinate every writer
sections.text: Use a cluster-aware filesystem or application and appropriate fencing. Mounting ordinary ext4/XFS concurrently can corrupt data.

remember: Shared blocks require coordinated writers.

title: Grow EBS deliberately; treat instance store as disposable
layout: Module 09 panels with functional conceptual diagrams

sections.heading: Resize persistent storage
sections.text: Supported size/type/performance changes are separate from extending the partition and filesystem in the guest OS.

sections.heading: Migrate to shrink
sections.text: EBS cannot shrink in place. Copy validated data to an appropriately smaller new volume, then perform a controlled cutover.

sections.heading: Protect host-local data
sections.text: Instance-store disks have instance-defined capacity and high local I/O. Use them for recreated scratch/cache; back up or replicate irreplaceable data.

remember: Persist required data beyond the lifetime of its host.

title: EFS shares files across clients and AZs
layout: Module 09 panels with functional conceptual diagrams

sections.heading: Managed shared NFS
sections.text: NFSv4.1 and POSIX semantics suit Linux applications that require concurrent shared-file access; EFS is not native Windows SMB.

sections.heading: Regional or One Zone
sections.text: Regional storage spans AZs; One Zone accepts a single-AZ boundary. File capacity grows automatically, but network and performance planning remain.

sections.heading: Choose a file workload
sections.text: CMS, WordPress, web serving and shared application content are common fits. Pay for used storage and applicable access/throughput features.

remember: Choose shared-file semantics and the right failure boundary.

title: A mount target is the network doorway to EFS
layout: Module 09 panels with functional conceptual diagrams

sections.heading: Mount-target network path
sections.text: Allow NFS TCP 2049 between the client and mount-target security groups; verify subnets, routes and return traffic.

sections.heading: Keep the path local
sections.text: Use an available mount target in the client AZ to avoid unnecessary cross-AZ paths. Mount-target availability differs for One Zone.

sections.heading: Extend private connectivity
sections.text: DX/VPN or supported VPC connectivity needs working DNS resolution or explicit target addressing. Provide redundant links and endpoints where required.

remember: A correct mount needs a working private path in both directions.

title: EFS authorization has several independent layers
layout: Module 09 panels with functional conceptual diagrams

sections.heading: Network and IAM gates
sections.text: Security groups provide reachability. Authenticated NFS mounts use the EFS helper and relevant IAM filesystem/client policies.

sections.heading: POSIX file permissions
sections.text: File UID/GID and directory read/write/execute permissions remain meaningful; IAM authorization does not replace POSIX checks.

sections.heading: Access-point identity
sections.text: Enforce an application root directory and identity. Restrict access-point use in policy; TLS protects transit and KMS protects stored data.

remember: Reachability, IAM and POSIX permissions solve different access questions.

title: Choose EFS throughput to match demand
layout: Module 09 panels with functional conceptual diagrams

sections.heading: Choose the performance mode
sections.text: General Purpose is the recommended low-latency mode. Previous-generation Max I/O has higher operation latency and configuration restrictions.

sections.heading: Match variable demand
sections.text: Elastic throughput follows changing demand without requiring stored capacity to purchase throughput.

sections.heading: Provision or use credits
sections.text: Provisioned sets throughput separately from capacity. Bursting earns/spends credits based on Standard-class bytes; read metering differs from writes.

remember: Choose a throughput mechanism that matches demand.

title: EFS lifecycle changes cost and access behavior
layout: Module 09 panels with functional conceptual diagrams

sections.heading: Choose the access tier
sections.text: Standard serves frequent file access; IA and Archive lower storage cost for less-used eligible files through lifecycle policies.

sections.heading: Model the complete cost
sections.text: Include retrieval/access costs, minimum durations, eligibility and latency. A lower storage rate does not guarantee a lower total bill.

sections.heading: Respect the AZ boundary
sections.text: Regional supports Archive; One Zone has a different class set. Automatic backups and restore readiness must fit the accepted failure boundary.

remember: Model access and recovery costs with storage costs.

title: EFS replication is asynchronous recovery
layout: Module 09 panels with functional conceptual diagrams

sections.heading: Asynchronous copy
sections.text: Initial synchronization must finish before the destination data is available. Continued replication is asynchronous.

sections.heading: Protected destination
sections.text: The active destination is protected against application writes; prepare its mount targets, key access and policies before failover.

sections.heading: Recover the application
sections.text: Monitor TimeSinceLastSync and test a deliberate writable failover and client remount. Replication does not preserve an independent backup history.

remember: Monitor the recovery point and prove the failover steps.

title: Choose FSx by filesystem semantics
layout: Module 09 panels with functional conceptual diagrams

sections.heading: Windows file semantics
sections.text: Windows File Server: SMB and Active Directory.

sections.heading: Parallel compute
sections.text: Lustre: parallel compute and S3-linked datasets.

sections.heading: ONTAP or OpenZFS
sections.text: ONTAP: NFS, SMB and iSCSI; OpenZFS: managed NFS with ZFS capabilities.

remember: Start with protocol and application semantics.

title: Windows file shares keep Windows access controls
layout: Module 09 panels with functional conceptual diagrams

sections.heading: Native Windows access
sections.text: SMB with native NTFS semantics supports traditional enterprise shares, home directories and compatible Windows applications.

sections.heading: Directory and permissions
sections.text: Integrate Microsoft AD for authentication and use ACLs, quotas and DFS Namespaces to manage access and file organization.

sections.heading: Compatible private clients
sections.text: Linux needs a compatible SMB client. On-premises access needs private routing, DNS and AD connectivity over supported DX/VPN paths.

remember: Windows file access needs both directory and network design.

title: Multi-AZ Windows file storage protects the server tier
layout: Module 09 panels with functional conceptual diagrams

sections.heading: Active and standby servers
sections.text: Managed Multi-AZ deployments keep active and standby Windows file servers in different AZs.

sections.heading: Reconnect after failover
sections.text: Failover changes the serving node; applications must tolerate the interruption and reconnect through supported names.

sections.heading: Keep recovery history
sections.text: FSx-managed automatic daily backups are enabled by default. They preserve recovery history; Multi-AZ alone does not reverse a mistaken delete.

remember: Availability replicas and historical backups protect different failures.

title: Change Windows file-system layout through migration
layout: Module 09 panels with functional conceptual diagrams

sections.heading: Create the target layout
sections.text: For a different AZ deployment or smaller allocated filesystem, provision a compatible new target.

sections.heading: Copy and validate
sections.text: Use a supported backup restore or DataSync migration. A backup restore is not a general way to shrink storage; migrate to a smaller target instead.

sections.heading: Cut over deliberately
sections.text: Stage the copy, pause writes, perform final synchronization, validate ACLs/data and switch application paths or DNS aliases.

remember: Plan migration and cutover before changing the storage layout.

title: Lustre feeds parallel compute
layout: Module 09 panels with functional conceptual diagrams

sections.heading: Parallel shared files
sections.text: Lustre provides concurrent shared-file access for HPC, ML, video processing, financial modeling and engineering workloads.

sections.heading: Compute and storage together
sections.text: Select storage media and throughput for metadata, small/random I/O or large/sequential I/O; benchmark the parallel workload.

sections.heading: Link durable source data
sections.text: Supported S3 repository linkage enables file processing without making S3 itself a general POSIX filesystem. Private hybrid clients still need supported connectivity.

remember: Parallel compute needs an appropriate shared-data path.

title: Lustre durability depends on deployment and storage type
layout: Module 09 panels with functional conceptual diagrams

sections.heading: Scratch is recreatable
sections.text: Scratch does not replicate data or replace failed file servers. Keep inputs and valuable outputs independently recoverable.

sections.heading: Persistent SSD and HDD
sections.text: These persistent configurations replicate data within one AZ and replace failed file servers. Plan independent protection for an AZ failure.

sections.heading: Persistent Intelligent-Tiering
sections.text: Current Intelligent-Tiering replicates data across multiple AZs. Data durability and filesystem serving availability are different properties; test application recovery.

remember: Specify deployment and storage type before describing the failure boundary.

title: Lazy loading brings the working set to Lustre
layout: Module 09 panels with functional conceptual diagrams

sections.heading: Import the namespace
sections.text: Linked S3 metadata can be imported before all file content is present in Lustre.

sections.heading: Load data on demand
sections.text: Reads fetch the needed file data, allowing a job to start without downloading the complete repository; retained working data reduces repeated fetches.

sections.heading: Export results explicitly
sections.text: Configure automatic import/export or explicit repository tasks as supported. Changed output reaches S3 only through the configured export behavior.

remember: Import and export behavior must be configured deliberately.

title: ONTAP combines file and block protocols
layout: Module 09 panels with functional conceptual diagrams

sections.heading: Serve file and block clients
sections.text: Storage virtual machines and volumes expose NFS, SMB and iSCSI to compatible Linux, Windows, macOS and application clients.

sections.heading: Protect and clone data
sections.text: Snapshots, replication, efficient clones, compression and deduplication support migration and testing; changed data can consume additional space.

sections.heading: Manage storage tiers
sections.text: Manage SSD capacity, IOPS and capacity-pool tiering separately. Automatic tiering is not unlimited capacity or an unconditional automatic-shrink promise.

remember: Tiering, capacity and high availability are separate controls.

title: OpenZFS brings ZFS capabilities to managed NFS
layout: Module 09 panels with functional conceptual diagrams

sections.heading: Managed NFS access
sections.text: OpenZFS exposes supported NFS v3/v4 variants; compatible clients need the right protocol, DNS and network permissions.

sections.heading: Snapshots and clones
sections.text: Point-in-time snapshots and writable clones support data recovery and safe testing. Compression saves space only where data compresses.

sections.heading: Provision the failure model
sections.text: Select Single-AZ or Multi-AZ capabilities, throughput and capacity deliberately. Managed service operations do not replace application-level recovery design.

remember: A snapshot, a clone and a deployment choice solve different jobs.

title: S3 File Gateway translates file access into objects
layout: Module 09 panels with functional conceptual diagrams

sections.heading: Translate NFS or SMB
sections.text: On-premises clients use NFS or SMB while the gateway stores file data as S3 objects.

sections.heading: Cache before asynchronous upload
sections.text: Local cache absorbs writes and serves active reads; cloud upload is asynchronous. Size the cache for the working set and dirty data.

sections.heading: Monitor object and cache behavior
sections.text: Watch upload completion and cache pressure. External S3 changes require supported refresh behavior; coordinate writers to avoid object conflicts.

remember: Local file access and asynchronous cloud durability are separate events.

title: Volume Gateway: decide where the primary data lives
layout: Module 09 panels with functional conceptual diagrams

sections.heading: Cached primary in AWS
sections.text: Cached volumes store primary data in managed AWS storage and retain a local working set.

sections.heading: Stored primary on premises
sections.text: Stored volumes keep the full primary dataset locally and back it up asynchronously to AWS.

sections.heading: Recover through snapshots
sections.text: Both expose iSCSI blocks. Plan local storage/upload buffers, snapshot recovery and connectivity; an EBS snapshot can restore a recovery volume.

remember: Locate the primary data before choosing the gateway mode.

title: Tape Gateway preserves the backup interface
layout: Module 09 panels with functional conceptual diagrams

sections.heading: Preserve the tape workflow
sections.text: Existing compatible backup software writes through an iSCSI virtual tape library rather than replacing its backup workflow.

sections.heading: Eject and archive
sections.text: Online virtual tapes are managed in S3-backed storage; ejected archived tapes use supported Glacier archive destinations with restore timing/cost.

sections.heading: Understand legacy alternatives
sections.text: FSx File Gateway is closed to new customers. Its historical SMB/local-cache design is distinct from S3 File Gateway and current new-deployment choices.

remember: Keep the tape interface while planning cloud retrieval behavior.

title: EBS walkthrough: modify, extend and verify
layout: Module 09 panels with functional conceptual diagrams

sections.heading: Inspect the sandbox volume
sections.text: Illustrative sandbox: inspect attachment, AZ, encryption, volume type and the instance EBS limits; take an appropriate recovery point.

sections.heading: Modify and extend
sections.text: Choose a supported volume modification. Wait for the required operation state and extend the guest partition/filesystem using OS-specific steps.

sections.heading: Verify and clean up
sections.text: Check lsblk/df and application behavior, validate the recovery point and remove sandbox resources. Never format an existing data volume just to expand it.

remember: Modify, extend and verify; never replace verification with a success icon.

title: EFS walkthrough: mount, authorize and prove sharing
layout: Module 09 panels with functional conceptual diagrams

sections.heading: Create the authorized path
sections.text: Illustrative sandbox: create a filesystem, suitable mount targets, a narrow TCP 2049 rule and configured application identity/access point.

sections.heading: Mount with TLS
sections.text: Install the EFS helper and mount with TLS plus the intended IAM/access-point options. Replace example IDs and check directory UID/GID permissions.

sections.heading: Prove sharing and denial
sections.text: Write/read a file from two authorized clients. Configure a separate denied policy or directory for the negative test; then unmount and clean up.

remember: Test both the intended allow and a deliberately configured deny.

title: A snapshot, an AMI and a regional recovery copy solve different jobs
layout: Module 09 panels with functional conceptual diagrams

sections.heading: Preserve volume blocks
sections.text: Snapshots preserve block data; a data-volume snapshot alone is not complete application boot metadata.

sections.heading: Define a bootable image
sections.text: An EBS-backed AMI references snapshots and includes relevant boot characteristics and block mappings. Instance type belongs to the launch decision/template.

sections.heading: Prepare regional recovery
sections.text: Copy snapshots or AMIs before a regional outage, authorize destination-region KMS keys and prove that a recovery instance can launch.

remember: An AMI supplies boot metadata; a launch template defines a launch configuration.

title: DLM owns the recovery points created by its policies
layout: Module 09 panels with functional conceptual diagrams

sections.heading: Select tagged resources
sections.text: Choose supported instance/volume targets using the policy's selection rules; custom schedules commonly use tags.

sections.heading: Manage policy-created backups
sections.text: DLM creates and retains snapshots or EBS-backed AMIs and applies configured lifecycle/copy actions.

sections.heading: Know the ownership boundary
sections.text: DLM does not take over arbitrary external snapshots or instance-store-backed AMIs. Wider supported-service governance belongs to AWS Backup.

remember: A lifecycle policy has a defined resource-ownership boundary.

title: Choose file-storage performance without changing its semantics
layout: Module 09 panels with functional conceptual diagrams

sections.heading: Windows SSD or HDD
sections.text: Windows SSD suits latency-sensitive or metadata-heavy access; HDD can fit suitable sequential, cost-sensitive shares.

sections.heading: Lustre I/O pattern
sections.text: Lustre performance depends on media, throughput and the degree of concurrent compute demand, not just filesystem capacity.

sections.heading: Enterprise file features
sections.text: ONTAP/OpenZFS features preserve their filesystem semantics; select the correct client protocol, connectivity, deployment and protection model.

remember: Performance selection must preserve required file semantics.

title: Deploy a gateway with identity, cache and recovery in mind
layout: Module 09 panels with functional conceptual diagrams

sections.heading: Separate client and bucket identity
sections.text: S3 File Gateway uses an IAM role for bucket access; SMB can authenticate users through Active Directory.

sections.heading: Size gateway resources
sections.text: File Gateway allocates local disks as cache, including dirty uploads. Separate upload-buffer requirements belong to other gateway types; size resources for the selected type.

sections.heading: Choose supported deployment
sections.text: Choose supported virtual host deployment. The historical AWS hardware appliance is no longer sold, and FSx File Gateway is unavailable to new customers.

remember: Client authentication, bucket authorization and local resources need separate plans.

title: Snapshot capture: protect the application's state

sections.heading: Coordinate writes
sections.text: A snapshot captures block storage, not an arbitrary database transaction. Flush writes, pause or quiesce applications as appropriate, and coordinate related volumes.

sections.heading: Detach is not mandatory
sections.text: A volume can remain attached while a snapshot is created. For stronger consistency, use a supported application-consistent procedure rather than assuming every attached snapshot is complete.

sections.heading: Schedule around real load
sections.text: Snapshot activity and application I/O share resources. Plan capture windows, monitor application impact and test restoration before relying on the recovery point.

remember: Consistency comes from the capture procedure and a tested restore.
layout: Module 09 panels with functional conceptual diagrams

title: Snapshot initialization: choose the recovery mechanism

sections.heading: Manual read initialization
sections.text: Read the restored device's blocks with a supported fio or dd procedure when appropriate. Read into /dev/null; do not overwrite production data during initialization.

sections.heading: Fast Snapshot Restore
sections.text: Enable FSR for the required snapshot/AZ pairs. It has eligibility, performance and volume-creation-credit limits plus additional charges.

sections.heading: Provisioned initialization
sections.text: A supported provisioned initialization rate gives more predictable block-download timing at extra cost. Specifying it overrides FSR for that volume; monitor initialization before application tests.

remember: Compare recovery timing, limits and cost rather than assuming every restored volume is warm.
layout: Module 09 panels with functional conceptual diagrams

title: EFS access points: give each application its own view

sections.heading: Enforce identity
sections.text: Example: application A uses UID/GID 2101 through access point A. EFS can replace the client-supplied POSIX identity with the access-point identity.

sections.heading: Override the root
sections.text: Access point A exposes /app-a as the client root; application B uses a separate /app-b root and identity. Configure directory ownership and permissions correctly.

sections.heading: Authorize the entry point
sections.text: Use filesystem/IAM conditions to restrict the allowed access point and require the intended TLS/IAM mount. An access point does not remove the need for network or POSIX permissions.

remember: A scoped directory view and an enforced identity complement policy authorization.
layout: Module 09 panels with functional conceptual diagrams

title: EFS policy defaults: do not confuse network access with IAM

sections.heading: Understand the default
sections.text: Without a user-configured filesystem policy, network-reachable anonymous NFS clients are allowed by the default policy. POSIX permissions still apply.

sections.heading: Use authenticated mounts
sections.text: The EFS mount helper with IAM authorization evaluates relevant identity and filesystem policies. ClientMount, ClientWrite and ClientRootAccess represent different permissions.

sections.heading: Restrict deliberately
sections.text: Enforce TLS and the intended principals/access points; configure root access appropriately. Test allowed and denied mounts after policy propagation.

remember: IAM is an explicit client authorization design, not an automatic replacement for NFS permissions.
layout: Module 09 panels with functional conceptual diagrams

title: EFS burst credits: connect storage size to throughput

sections.heading: Earn the baseline
sections.text: Bursting throughput earns credits according to Standard-class storage. A larger Standard working set can earn a higher baseline; cold-class bytes do not purchase the same baseline.

sections.heading: Spend credits on peaks
sections.text: Unused baseline accumulates credits. Demand above baseline spends them; after depletion, sustained performance follows the available baseline and applicable limits.

sections.heading: Separate read metering
sections.text: Reads are metered differently from writes. Use the exact current formula and Region/client limits in the comparison reference; choose Elastic or Provisioned when the credit model does not fit.

remember: File capacity, metered throughput and application read rate are different measurements.
layout: Module 09 panels with functional conceptual diagrams

title: EFS replication: measure RPO and rehearse RTO

sections.heading: Finish the initial sync
sections.text: The initial copy depends on data size and file count; destination data is not available until that sync completes. It is not an instant empty-to-ready recovery.

sections.heading: Monitor the recovery point
sections.text: AWS targets a 15-minute RPO for most filesystems after initial sync, with documented workload exceptions. Track TimeSinceLastSync and the last replicated timestamp.

sections.heading: Test the complete failover
sections.text: A writable destination, mount targets, DNS, KMS/IAM access and application remounts determine practical RTO. Replication uses managed capacity and does not consume the source's provisioned throughput allocation.

remember: An RPO target is not a guarantee of application recovery time.
layout: Module 09 panels with functional conceptual diagrams

title: File Gateway data can feed cloud processing

sections.heading: Upload then process
sections.text: NFS/SMB clients write through the local gateway to S3. Trigger downstream work only when the intended object/upload is ready; local close alone is not proof of completed cloud upload.

sections.heading: Extend the workflow
sections.text: S3 events can invoke Lambda, while Athena, Redshift Spectrum or EMR consume supported datasets from S3. Handle duplicated events and concurrent changes in the consumer design.

sections.heading: Replicate deliberately
sections.text: Supported S3 replication can move objects to another bucket/Region. Validate versioning, permissions and destination access; replication does not coordinate multiple gateway writers.

remember: A file bridge can feed object workflows without turning every consumer into a shared filesystem client.
layout: Module 09 panels with functional conceptual diagrams

title: Read-only gateway replicas need refresh and writer discipline

sections.heading: Choose one writer
sections.text: Use one authoritative write share for an object set. Multiple gateways writing the same objects can create conflicts; a shared bucket is not a distributed file-lock manager.

sections.heading: Expose read-only shares
sections.text: Other sites can use read-only gateway shares backed by the intended S3 data. Network/file permissions and gateway caching still control what readers see.

sections.heading: Refresh the inventory
sections.text: External changes need supported cache refresh or refresh settings. RefreshCache updates cached object inventory, not a full eager download; wait for completion before validating new files.

remember: Read-only distribution still needs freshness, authorization and a defined writer.
layout: Module 09 panels with functional conceptual diagrams

title: File Gateway backups: lifecycle, versions and WORM

sections.heading: Tier backup objects
sections.text: A backup application can write files through the gateway to S3. Apply deliberate Standard/IA/archive lifecycle and retention rules, including retrieval time and minimum-duration charges.

sections.heading: Recover a previous version
sections.text: Versioning can retain overwritten objects. Restore the intended object version through S3, then refresh the gateway inventory so file clients see the recovered state; test the recovery workflow.

sections.heading: Retain protected versions
sections.text: S3 Object Lock protects eligible object versions with retention or legal hold. A client modification can create a new version; it does not rewrite an already protected version.

remember: Lifecycle, version history and immutable retention protect different recovery requirements.
layout: Module 09 panels with functional conceptual diagrams

title: Gateway recovery: restore the correct storage interface

sections.heading: Recover block volumes
sections.text: Volume Gateway exposes iSCSI. Its cloud snapshot recovery can create an EBS volume for an EC2 recovery workload; adapt the application and validate data consistency.

sections.heading: Retrieve virtual tapes
sections.text: Tape Gateway presents an iSCSI virtual tape library. Ejection and archive change retrieval time and cost; use compatible backup software to retrieve and restore the tape data.

sections.heading: Protect the whole path
sections.text: Use supported encrypted cloud transport over internet or private connectivity. Local cache, upload buffers and host resources depend on gateway type; loss of unuploaded data remains a separate risk.

remember: Recovery must reproduce the application's required interface and usable data.
layout: Module 09 panels with functional conceptual diagrams

title: Lustre Intelligent-Tiering changes the storage comparison

sections.heading: Elastic storage
sections.text: Persistent Intelligent-Tiering grows with stored data and moves eligible data among Frequent Access, Infrequent Access and Archive Instant Access tiers.

sections.heading: Choose throughput and cache
sections.text: Throughput is provisioned separately; an optional SSD read cache accelerates eligible reads. This differs from the SSD or HDD capacity-based comparison in older course tables.

sections.heading: Keep recovery explicit
sections.text: Intelligent-Tiering replicates data across multiple AZs. Do not translate that durability feature into an unqualified promise of continuous client access or application disaster recovery.

remember: Keep historical PDF figures separate from the current configuration's documented capabilities.
layout: Module 09 panels with functional conceptual diagrams
